summary:
Orbivia is a health monitoring and decision-support system for astronaut crews on short and long missions. Every day it merges biometric, sleep, cognitive (PVT-B), behavioral and social signals into one state vector per astronaut and compares it with that person’s own baseline, never a population average. Alerts fire only when evidence converges (sustained ±2σ deviations, negative trends or combined signals), and it flags the gap between how tired astronauts say they feel and how they actually perform. Each morning it proposes three explainable task plans within NASA-STD-3001 workload limits; the commander chooses after consulting the crew.

The challenge asks astronauts to monitor their own health, but NASA’s evidence shows why that is hard: sleep loss impairs the very ability to notice decline, and psychological and team risks are only accepted if someone watches them, turning red on Mars missions. Orbivia does that watching on board and autonomously, with role-based access, pseudonymized data, no stored audio or video, and a human always making the final call. Far from Earth, catching problems early is the difference between adjusting a schedule and losing a crew member’s capability.
details:
What it does and how it works
Orbivia is a health monitoring and decision-support system for the whole crew on short and long space missions. It tracks physiological data (heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, grip strength, sleep, radiation dose), cognitive performance (a daily 3-minute PVT-B reaction-time test), a daily 5-question check-in (sleep, tiredness, workload, mood, team life), short open audio interviews and social signals such as sleep desynchronization and isolation during free time.

Each day, all these signals are merged into one state vector per astronaut. The vector is compared with that astronaut’s own baseline, never with a population average. That baseline comes from a 6-month pre-flight Earth baseline, which is frozen so slow decline can’t shift it, plus an adaptation baseline from the first days in microgravity. Alerts only fire when the evidence converges: a deviation beyond ±2σ that lasts 3 days, a sustained negative trend, or several signals getting worse together. Orbivia also flags the “self-perception gap”, when an astronaut says they feel fine but their reaction time says otherwise. NASA-archived research (Van Dongen et al., 2003) shows sleep-deprived people barely notice their own decline.

Orbivia goes beyond the challenge. Instead of only showing data, it tries to prevent a fatigued astronaut from getting worse. Every morning it proposes three alternative plans for common and maintenance tasks, so more demanding work goes to the crew members in better condition. Each plan respects NASA-STD-3001 workload limits, rest and fixed exercise time, and comes with a plain-language explanation of every change. The commander picks one after consulting the crew, or rejects them all. Orbivia never decides on its own.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Early detection of fatigue, psychological and team problems, which NASA rates as risks that need monitoring even on short missions and as red on Mars-class missions.
    • Audio and video are processed in memory and never stored.
    • Identity is kept separate from biometric data.
    • Access depends on role: each astronaut sees their own measurements, the flight surgeon sees medical details, and the commander only sees an availability score with a general reason.

Tools and technologies

  • Backend: Python with FastAPI and role-based access control, PostgreSQL 16 with pgvector, and Redis Streams for continuous sleep data.
  • Task planning: Google OR-Tools CP-SAT optimizer.
  • Audio, text and video: openSMILE (eGeMAPS) for voice features, faster-whisper for transcription with an optional text classifier, and MediaPipe + ONNX for physical signs of fatigue such as eye closure and slow blinking.
  • Frontend: framework-free HTML/CSS/JS served by Nginx.
  • Infrastructure: fully containerized with Docker Compose, including a simulated Earth link. A static demo is published on GitHub Pages.
  • Data: a reproducible simulated mission calibrated with values NASA publishes for spaceflight.

What makes it creative

  • It compares each astronaut with themselves, and catches what self-reporting misses through the self-perception gap.
  • A weekly “double question” (“how do you think the rest of the crew will rate team life?”) reveals social disconnection. It is inspired by the Bayesian Truth Serum.
  • It turns monitoring into concrete, explainable decisions about who should do which task.

Factors we considered

  • NASA evidence: the Human Research Program risk tables, NASA-STD-3001, the PVT-B and Cognition tests, and NASA Ames’ Playbook.
  • Microgravity adaptation: a separate adaptation baseline so the system doesn’t raise alerts for everyone right after launch.
  • Human oversight: a person always makes the final decision.
  • Regulation: GDPR and the EU AI Act. Emotion inference is limited to medical use.
  • Explainability: rule-based optimization rather than a trained model, because no real in-flight astronaut data exists to train one.
  • Psychological wellbeing: astronauts don’t see their own alert labels. The flight surgeon handles them.
dataRefs: NASA HRR – Sleep Loss and Work Overload Risk
